source_text: (Sed Christus diuortium inhibet dicens: qui dimiserit uxorem suam et aliam duxerit, adulterium committet, (et) qui dimissam a uiro duxerit, aeque adulter est, - ut sic quoque prohibeat diuortium, inlicitum facit repudiatae matrimonium — Moyses uero permittit repudium in Deuteronomio: si sumserit quis uxorem et habitauerit cum ea, et euenerit non inuenire eam apud eum gratiam, eo quod inuentum sit in illa impudicum negotium, scribet libellum repudii et dabit in manu eius et dimittet illam de domo sua. uides diuersitatem legis et euangelii, Moysi et Christi\'? plane. non enim recepisti illud quoque euangelium eiusdem ueritatis et eiusdem Christi, in quo prohibens diuortium propriam quaestionem eius absoluit: Moyses propter duritiam cordis uestri praecepit libellum repudii dare; a primordio autem non fuit sic; quia scilicet qui marem et feminam fecerat, erunt duo, dixerat, in carne una; quod deus itaque iunxit, homo (non) disiunxerit. hoc enim responso et Moysi constitutionem protexit, ut sui, et creatoris institutionem direxit, ut Christus ipsius. sed quatenus ex his reuincendus es, quae recepisti, sic tibi occurram, ac si meus Christus (tuus:) nonne et ipse prohibens diuortium et parem tamen gestans eius, qui marem et feminam iunxit, excusauerit potius quam destruxerit Moysi constitutionem? sed ecce sic tuus sit iste Christus contrarium docens Moysi et creatori, ut, si non contrarium ostendero, meus sit. dico enim illum condicionaliter nunc fecisse diuortii prohibitionem, si ideo quis dimittat uxoiem, ut aliam ducat: qui dimiserit, inquit, uxorem et aliam duxerit, adulterium commisit, et qui a marito dimissam duxerit aeque adulter est, ex eadem utique causa dimissam, qua non licet dimitti, ut alia ducatur; inlicite enim dimissam pro indimissa ducens adulter est. manet enim matrimonium quod non rite diremptum est; manente (autem) matrimonio nubere adulterium est. ita si condicionaliter prohibuit dimittere uxorem, non in totum prohibuit, et quod non prohibuit in totum, permisit alias, ubi causa cessat, ob quam prohibuit;
pass_a_gloss: But Christ forbids divorce, saying: he who dismisses his wife and marries another, commits adultery, and he who marries a woman dismissed by her husband, is equally an adulterer, - so that in this way also He forbids divorce, making the marriage of a divorced woman unlawful — Moses, however, permits divorce in Deuteronomy: if someone takes a wife and lives with her, and it happens that he does not find favor with her, because some indecent matter is found in her, he shall write a bill of divorce and give it to her hand and dismiss her from his house. You see the difference between the law and the gospel, of Moses and Christ? Indeed. For you have not received that gospel of the same truth and the same Christ, in which, forbidding divorce, He resolves His own question: Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, commanded to give a bill of divorce; but from the beginning it was not so; because, indeed, He who made the male and the female, said: the two shall be one flesh; what God has joined, let man not separate. For by this response, He both protected Moses' constitution, as His own, and directed the institution of the Creator, as Christ Himself. But insofar as you are to be convinced by these things, which you have received, I shall meet you as if my Christ were yours: does He not, while forbidding divorce and yet bearing the same attitude as He who joined the male and the female, excuse rather than destroy Moses' constitution? But behold, if your Christ is such, teaching the opposite of Moses and the Creator, so that, if I do not show the opposite, He is mine. For I say that He conditionally made the prohibition of divorce, if someone dismisses his wife in order to marry another: he who dismisses his wife and marries another, commits adultery, and he who marries a woman dismissed by her husband, is equally an adulterer, for the same reason for which it is not lawful to dismiss her, in order to marry another; for he who marries a unlawfully dismissed woman, as if she were not dismissed, is an adulterer. For the marriage remains which has not been lawfully dissolved; and while the marriage remains, to marry is adultery. Thus, if He conditionally forbade dismissing a wife, He did not forbid it altogether, and what He did not forbid altogether, He permitted in other cases, where the reason for which He forbade it ceases to exist;
pass_b_english: Christ forbids divorce: "Anyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and the man who marries a divorced woman is equally an adulterer." He makes remarriage after divorce unlawful, thereby forbidding divorce itself. Moses, however, permits divorce in Deuteronomy: if a man takes a wife, lives with her, then finds no favor in her because he discovers something indecent, he writes a certificate of divorce, hands it to her, and sends her away (Deut 24:1–4). You see the clash between the Law and the Gospel, between Moses and Christ? Of course you do. You haven't accepted that Gospel—the same truth, the same Christ—in which, while forbidding divorce, he settles his own question: "Moses, because of your hard hearts, allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so. The Creator made them male and female, and said, ‘The two shall become one flesh.’ So what God has joined together, let no one separate" (Matt 19:8–6; Gen 2:24). By that answer he both shields Moses' statute as his own and upholds the Creator's institution as Christ's own.

Now, to convict you on the grounds you actually accept, I'll meet you on your own turf—as if my Christ were yours. Doesn't he, while forbidding divorce, still share the mind of the One who joined male and female, and therefore *excuse* Moses' law rather than destroy it? But look: if your Christ teaches the opposite of Moses and the Creator, then he's mine—unless I can prove the opposite. I say he imposed the ban *conditionally*: "If a man divorces his wife *in order to marry another*, he commits adultery; and whoever marries a woman divorced *on that ground* is likewise an adulterer, because the original marriage was never lawfully dissolved. As long as that marriage stands, remarrying is adultery." So if the prohibition is conditional, it's not total; and what isn't totally forbidden is permitted in cases where the reason for the ban disappears.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the conditional nature of Christ's prohibition and the distinction between Moses' law and Christ's teaching. Scripture citations (Deut 24:1–4, Matt 19:8–6, Gen 2:24) are correctly added to the English text to identify the quoted/alluded passages as required. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Latin source.
